kp.k: Study compares expected and actual AI-assisted task performance
kp.d: Yu and colleagues report a preregistered behavioral study in an arXiv preprint dated 22 May 2026. The reported sample was N=1237: 401 in the prediction sample and 836 in the completion sample, recruited through Prolific. Participants predicted independent and assisted completion times or completed tasks independently or using an embedded GPT-4o chat interface. The 24 tasks covered information seeking, information processing and synthesis, procedural guidance and execution, and content creation and transformation, at two difficulty levels. This is cross-domain evidence about human–AI interaction, not a study of legal work.

kp.k: Participants expected greater time savings from AI than humans
kp.d: Participants predicted AI assistance would reduce completion times by 68.5 seconds (SE = 3.37, p < 0.001), compared with 17.10 seconds for assistance from another participant described as highly intelligent (SE = 3.36, p < 0.001). They expected speedups on 18 tasks with AI versus five with human assistance and expressed stronger preferences for AI assistance. The human comparison concerned hypothetical predictions; the completion experiment did not measure actual human-assisted performance.

kp.k: AI-assisted completion times were systematically underestimated
kp.d: Actual AI-assisted completion took 57.8 seconds longer than predicted (SE = 8.79, p < 0.001). The authors report this speedup illusion across all four task categories and both difficulty levels. Independent completion predictions showed no significant aggregate discrepancy from actual times (β = −2.52, SE = 8.83, p = 0.775), although participants underestimated independent times for information processing and synthesis and overestimated them for content creation and transformation. The finding concerns aggregate calibration rather than each individual's forecasting accuracy.

kp.k: Time savings depended on task difficulty and type
kp.d: The abstract reports no overall difference between independent and AI-assisted completion times. The detailed results qualify this: AI assistance reduced completion time on difficult tasks by 26.14 seconds (SE = 11.9, p < 0.05), but not on easy tasks. Significant task-specific speedups occurred for generating ten alternatives to “enjoy,” summarizing a long article, and editing a long text. Separately, the authors report a significant slowdown on the logic task; therefore, the three speedups should not be interpreted as the only significant task-level time effects.

kp.k: Reduced subjective effort did not imply reduced completion time
kp.d: AI assistance reduced average subjective workload by 0.61 points on a seven-point NASA-TLX scale (SE = 0.059, p < 0.001), with statistically significant reductions on 15 of 24 tasks. Completion time and average NASA-TLX were only weakly positively correlated (r = 0.26). Although the authors describe effort reduction across all tasks, statistical significance was not established for every task. They propose conflation of effort savings with time savings as a possible explanation for the speedup illusion, rather than demonstrating that causal mechanism.

kp.k: Thinking aversion correlated with stronger expected AI speedups
kp.d: Responses to two Need for Cognition items associated greater aversion to thinking with larger predicted AI time savings: item 3 had β = −6.55, SE = 3.14, p < 0.05; item 4 had β = −6.66, SE = 3.19, p < 0.05. AI-use frequency and the AIAS measure did not predict calibration-error magnitude. These are reported associations, not evidence that aversion causes miscalibration or that additional AI experience cannot improve it.

kp.k: Prompting and processing responses consumed time despite rapid generation
kp.d: More than 70% of AI interactions were single-turn, with at most five turns; 18.5% of prompts directly copied task instructions. Copying did not significantly reduce completion time but reduced average NASA-TLX by 0.14 points (SE = 0.058, p < 0.05). Model generation averaged 2.89 seconds. Overall prompting and post-response processing times did not significantly differ, although prompting took 33.4 seconds longer for information-processing tasks. On the logic problem, post-response processing took 113.9 seconds longer than prompting; AI-assisted completion was 110.66 seconds slower despite predicted savings of 136.31 seconds. The authors connect this example to verbose, difficult-to-understand responses.

kp.k: AI assistance involved varied degrees of cognitive engagement
kp.d: Qualitative interaction analysis found participants using AI for recall, confirmation, expansion of existing answers, articulation of reasons, and summarization, rather than uniformly delegating whole tasks. Some had already performed much of the cognitive work before receiving an AI response. Participants also challenged omissions and requested explanations. The authors interpret these behaviors as evidence that AI use can include active thinking and potentially resource-rational choices, not simply passive substitution.

kp.k: Overreliance feedback loops remain a proposed downstream risk
kp.d: The authors argue that overestimated time savings could encourage delegation, while experienced effort savings could reinforce miscalibration and further AI use. Drawing on other studies, they warn that excessive offloading could cause deskilling, slower independent performance, cognitive surrender, and overreliance. They describe their feedback-loop evidence as preliminary; this experiment does not establish longitudinal skill loss or a self-reinforcing adoption cycle. They recommend considering effort alongside time in productivity assessments and studying calibration as a potential intervention.

kp.k: Short tasks and sample design constrain interpretation
kp.d: The study focused on tasks completable in under five minutes. Analyses excluded incorrect, low-effort, and nonresponsive answers: 6.3% of independent-condition responses and 4.0% of AI-assisted responses. Motivation and incentives were not directly controlled, and crowdworking may differ from higher-stakes settings. AI-use strategies varied, assigned completion modes did not reveal natural adoption choices, and calibration relied on between-subject aggregates with some overlap between prediction and completion samples. The authors call for research on complexity thresholds, incentives, voluntary AI use, and within-subject calibration.

pts.k: Yu and colleagues claim that AI assistance can reduce perceived cognitive effort without producing corresponding time savings, creating a 'speedup illusion' in simple cognitive tasks.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of human–AI interaction, not legal services. The authors report that participants expected AI assistance to save 68.5 seconds, but actual AI-assisted completion took 57.8 seconds longer than predicted. Independent completion predictions were approximately accurate in aggregate, although category-level exceptions occurred. The authors report no overall completion-time advantage, but a 26.14-second advantage on difficult tasks and significant speedups on three individual tasks: generating synonyms, summarizing a long article, and editing a long text. AI reduced average subjective effort by 0.61 points on a seven-point NASA-TLX scale; reductions were statistically significant for 15 of 24 tasks. They propose, rather than establish causally, that users confuse effort savings with time savings. They also suggest that miscalibration, increased AI use, and experienced effort savings could reinforce one another, potentially fostering overreliance and deskilling. Their qualitative observations also identify active, thoughtful uses of AI rather than uniformly passive delegation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw on a preregistered behavioral experiment, timing and subjective-effort measurements, mixed-effects analyses, and qualitative examination of GPT-4o interactions; longer-term risks remain proposed mechanisms.
pts.d: The paper reports N = 1,237 participants: 401 in a prediction sample and 836 in a completion sample. Participants predicted independent and assisted completion times, or completed tasks independently or using an embedded GPT-4o interface. The authors constructed 24 tasks across information seeking, processing and synthesis, procedural guidance and execution, and content creation and transformation, with easy and difficult versions. Completion times were recorded with hidden timers; subjective effort was measured using five NASA-TLX questions. Analyses excluded incorrect, low-effort, or nonresponsive answers: 6.3% of independent responses and 4.0% of AI-assisted responses. The authors used mixed-effects models and examined conversation histories. Model generation averaged 2.89 seconds, while prompting and processing responses accounted for additional time. A logic task illustrated how verbose answers could increase completion time. Copying instructions into prompts was associated with lower effort, not significantly shorter completion time. Greater aversion to thinking was associated with larger anticipated AI savings, whereas AI-use frequency and the AIAS measure did not predict calibration error. The human-assistance comparison measured expectations only: there was no actual human-assisted completion condition. The proposed effort-confusion mechanism and feedback loop were not directly established through longitudinal or causal testing.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical findings concern immediate performance on short tasks using GPT-4o; no timetable is given for possible overreliance or deskilling.
pts.d: The supplied source is an arXiv v1 paper dated 22 May 2026. Its experiment focuses on tasks that can be completed in under five minutes, not extended professional workflows. Miscalibration is reported across all four task categories and both difficulty levels, but actual time savings differ by task and difficulty. The authors acknowledge that motivation and incentives were not directly controlled, that crowdworking may differ from higher-stakes settings, and that AI use varied substantially between participants. Their between-subjects aggregate comparison does not directly measure each person's prediction error against their own performance, and some participants took part in both samples. Completion mode was assigned rather than freely chosen. The claim that AI always reduces effort is broader than the reported task-level significance, which covered 15 of 24 tasks. Potential feedback loops, deskilling, and calibration interventions are forward-looking suggestions with no specified duration or demonstrated long-term effect.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is US adult crowdworkers; the authors discuss implications for AI users and productivity assessment generally, not lawyers or legal markets.
pts.d: Participants were recruited through Prolific and described by the authors as representative of the US adult population. They performed short everyday cognitive tasks, including naming Olympic medalists, summarizing, editing, providing instructions, and constructing logical arguments. Users may experience less effort without saving time, and those more averse to thinking may anticipate larger time savings. Some users incur substantial prompting and response-processing costs; others use AI to recall, check, expand, or articulate ideas they have already developed. The authors argue that AI-productivity reporting should distinguish subjective effort from elapsed time and suggest calibration as a possible intervention against overreliance. The study provides no direct evidence about legal professionals, clients, staffing, pricing, or legal-service delivery.
